query: For high-entropy alloys intended for aerospace fasteners, what single intervention could improve the combination of mechanical durability, room-temperature creep resistance, and corrosion resistance? Formulate one hypothesis specifying the intervention, its mechanism, the predicted improvement relative to an untreated baseline, the conditions under which it should hold, prior evidence that supports it, and an experiment with clear results that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: Incorporating 5–10 wt% Mo into a NiCrCoFe-based high-entropy alloy will enhance its mechanical durability, room-temperature creep resistance, and corrosion resistance relative to the Mo-free baseline.
generation.material_initial_state: A NiCrCoFe high-entropy alloy produced via directed energy deposition (or a similar additive manufacturing process) without Mo addition.
generation.intervention: Add 5–10 wt% Mo to the alloy composition during fabrication.
generation.conditions: Tests conducted under ambient (room temperature) loading conditions for mechanical durability and creep, and in a 3.5 wt% NaCl solution for corrosion evaluation.
generation.structural_mediator: Formation of a solid-solution strengthened matrix and potential Mo-rich precipitates or surface layers, which modify grain boundary chemistry and microstructural stability.
generation.mechanism: Mo increases yield strength by impeding dislocation movement and may raise the activation energy for creep, thereby retarding room-temperature creep. Simultaneously, Mo contributes to forming protective surface oxides or enriched layers that improve corrosion resistance.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the untreated NiCrCoFe HEA, the Mo-modified alloy will exhibit a noticeable increase in tensile strength and durability, lower creep strain under long-term room-temperature loading, and a higher corrosion potential with a lower current density in a saline environment.
generation.baseline: NiCrCoFe HEA without Mo addition manufactured under identical processing conditions.
generation.boundary: The improvements are anticipated when the alloy is processed under conditions that ensure a homogeneous microstructure; deviations in cooling rates or processing defects may limit the benefits. Also, while mechanical and corrosion improvements are supported, the direct impact on room-temperature creep resistance remains less established.
generation.uncertainty: It is not yet fully determined if the Mo addition will effectively suppress room-temperature creep, as creep tests at ambient conditions are uncommon and may be influenced by additional microstructural factors.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples: a baseline NiCrCoFe HEA without Mo and a modified version with 5–10 wt% Mo, both manufactured via DED. Subject the samples to tensile tests for mechanical strength, long-duration static loading tests at room temperature to measure creep behavior, and potentiodynamic polarization tests in a 3.5 wt% NaCl solution to assess corrosion resistance.
measurements: Creep strain over an extended period at room temperature
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Mo-added samples do not display statistically significant improvements in tensile strength, a reduction in room-temperature creep strain, and enhanced corrosion metrics (higher Ecorr and lower Icorr) compared to the baseline, the hypothesis will be falsified.

## Abstract
AbstractHighly entropy alloys (HEAs) are novel materials that have great potential for application in aerospace and marine engineering due to their superior mechanical properties and benefits over conventional materials. NiCrCoFe, also referred to as Ni-based HEA, has exceptional low-temperature strength and microstructural stability. However, HEAs have limited corrosion resistance in some environments, such as a 3.5 wt% sodium chloride (NaCl) solution. Adding corrosion-resistant elements such as molybdenum (Mo) to HEAs is expected to increase their corrosion resistance in a variety of corrosive environments. Metal additive manufacturing reduces production times compared to casting and eliminates shrinkage issues, making it ideal for producing homogeneous HEA. This study used directed energy deposition (DED) to create Cr25-xCo25Ni25Fe25Mox (x = 0, 5, 10%) HEAs. Tensile strength and potentiodynamic polarization tests were used to assess the materials’ mechanical properties and corrosion resistance.
